prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which made atomic frequency standards at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a case where a simple and original idea, trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels, removed the central limitation of optical atomic clocks and opened a new regime of precision. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reproduced and compared by many independent laboratories with Sr, Yb and Hg, so the result is robust in exactly the sense I look for. The clocks resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres, constrain varying constants and dark-matter couplings, and are the leading route to a redefinition of the second. The credit is also unusually clean: Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations, Ye for taking the system to the accuracy frontier and for the many-body clock physics. Four of the seven members who ranked it placed it first or second, and I have moved it up from my sixth place after reading their arguments, because I find the case on maturity and attribution stronger than I first weighed it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology around frequency standards has been honoured before (Hall and Hansch 2005, Wineland and Haroche 2012), so the committee should ask whether lattice clocks are a new discovery or a very successful refinement of an established technique. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, which some colleagues may weigh as a missing milestone, and contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and other clock groups lie outside the two credited names. My own first choice, circuit QED (B023), is the area I know best, but I am wary of letting my field's proximity and the 2025 circuits prize drive the outcome, and the allocation among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff is genuinely unresolved.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because the magic-wavelength idea is simple, original and decisive, and because progress in physics is limited by how precisely we can measure; he also notes that the redefinition of the second is approaching.
responses.response: I agree with the substance, and the reproducibility across continents and species is what persuades me. I would qualify the argument that a redefinition is approaching: it is a policy decision, not a scientific criterion, and I would not let the committee count it as support. The prize should rest on the demonstrated 1e-18 performance and the physics it enables. I also take his point that Hall-Hansch and Wineland do not exclude this, but our citation should name the lattice and magic-wavelength concept explicitly to separate it from the comb and ion-clock prizes.

responses.point: Danielsson puts IceCube first as a genuine new window on the universe, with the diffuse flux, the TXS 0506+056 association and the Galactic-plane result providing sources, and argues that it is the kind of instrument-and-discovery story the committee has honoured.
responses.response: I accept that IceCube is a strong discovery and that I am the least qualified person here to judge the astrophysics. My concern is attribution: the diffuse flux is a collaboration result, and members propose either Halzen and Karle or a trio with Yoshida, and several colleagues (Olsson, Pearce, Kroll) themselves call the collaboration-scale credit a compromise. Lattice clocks have a much narrower and better-documented credit. If the committee can settle the Halzen-Karle-Yoshida question and the historical role of AMANDA, I would be willing to see IceCube as a serious competitor, perhaps even as a second part.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a prediction-then-confirmation story in which Bistritzer-MacDonald theory and Jarillo-Herrero's experiment fit quantitatively, and regards recognition as timely though perhaps slightly early.
responses.response: I find the theory-plus-experiment structure attractive and I keep B029 as an alternative. Where I would press is on whether the discovery is stable: the superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated, and Pearce raises the omission of Yuan Cao from the credited names as a fairness issue. I would ask whether the quantitative agreement for the flat bands is the same as understanding of the correlated states. Compared with clocks, which are reproduced to agreeing frequency ratios in many labs, the moire field is younger and I think it is probably one or two years early for a decisive recommendation.

responses.point: Pearce regards circuit QED as a natural successor to the 2025 recognition of circuits, but worries that a close follow-up might seem repetitive, and notes it is outside his own field so he relies on colleagues for the theory-experiment credit.
responses.response: As the one member who ranked circuit QED first, I should be candid about my bias and take his concern seriously. The 2025 prize was for macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation, which is a distinct discovery, but I agree that giving a second prize in superconducting circuits within a year invites the appearance of favouring one community. On credit, I disagree with the idea of leaving Blais out: the 2004 proposal was the theoretical basis, and Girvin has an equally strong claim, so the cap of three makes a convincing circuit QED prize harder than the clock prize. This is why I would not push B023 now.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Halperin-Nelson-Young theory of defect-mediated melting and the hexatic phase first as a clean, universal mechanism with confirmation over decades, and says recognition is, if anything, overdue.
responses.response: I defer to him on soft matter and statistical mechanics, and I see the elegance and the three-person fit. My question is about the 2016 prize for topological defects and phase transitions: if the committee judges that this melting theory is a distinct discovery, I am open to it. But with only him supporting it in the openings, I would want a second member with expertise in this area to say how much was new beyond Kosterlitz and Thouless, and whether the colloidal and simulation evidence settled the first-order versus continuous debate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as a new discovery or as a refinement of earlier precision-metrology prizes (2005, 2012).
Whether other clock pioneers (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others) change the fairness of a two-person credit.
How the committee should weigh the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize against circuit QED, and how to allocate credit among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff.
Whether IceCube credit can be settled among Halzen, Karle and Yoshida, which decides if it is a viable second part.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work at Chalmers MC2 in superconducting circuits, so I should recuse myself from decisions on circuit QED (B023) and probably from the superconducting-circuit areas B015 and B003. I have close ties to Per Delsing and Chris Wilson at Chalmers; none of the lattice-clock candidates (Katori, Ye) has a specific connection to me apparent from my profile, so no recusal is needed for B043.
